messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol is a 22-year-old accountant who came to treatment months after her four-year-old nephew was rushed to the hospital with a sudden, life-threatening infection. She had been the one watching him that afternoon in her sister’s apartment while her sister was at work. What she remembers most clearly is not a sequence she can easily tell from beginning to end, but flashes that still feel lodged in her body: his skin suddenly too hot under her hands, the unnatural quiet when he stopped crying and went limp against her shoulder, the metallic, sour taste of stale coffee and bile in the back of her throat as she waited for the ambulance and tried to keep him awake. Even now she says she cannot really “tell the story right.” When she starts to approach it, her mind jerks away before she can get to the worst part, and she is left with fragments rather than a complete account.

In the weeks after he survived and eventually recovered, Marisol found that certain moments pulled those fragments back with alarming force. Silence became especially hard to bear. If a room went unusually quiet, she would feel a rush of alarm before she even knew why, as if quiet itself meant that something terrible had already started. At work in the accounting office, when the usual tapping of keyboards stopped or a colleague took too long to answer from the next cubicle, her chest tightened and her stomach flipped. Delays had a similar effect. If her sister did not text back quickly, if a report took longer to load on her screen, if a call was placed on hold for too long, she was immediately certain that something bad was unfolding somewhere out of sight. In those moments her body reacted first—heart pounding, breath turning shallow, hands going cold—and the sensation brought her right back toward the hospital day. The taste would return to her mouth so vividly that she would swallow hard and look around in confusion, and then just as quickly she would force the whole memory back down before it could fully form.

Because the memory came back in this broken, wordless way, Marisol had come to believe something bleak about herself and her life. The fact that she could not put the event into words made it feel less like something finished in the past and more like proof that she had never really escaped it. When she shut the memory down before it was complete, she was left with the rawest pieces—her nephew limp, the waiting, the taste in her mouth—and those pieces seemed to confirm what frightened her most: that she could not stop bad things from happening. She said she used to be a happy person, easy with friends and quick to laugh, but now she felt miserable in a steady, flattened way that she could not shake. Around other people her age, especially coworkers talking casually about weekend plans, she felt set apart, as though everyone else had been allowed to remain young while she had learned too early that disaster could arrive without warning.

That sense of danger has narrowed her life. At the office she checks her phone repeatedly for messages from family, and when a reply is delayed she can no longer focus on spreadsheets because her mind has already leapt to the emergency room. If the floor around her falls silent, she feels the same surge of dread and the same bodily jolt, followed by those sensory scraps of the day her nephew nearly died. She tries to interrupt it by keeping background noise on, stepping to the restroom, getting water, anything to avoid letting the memory gather enough shape to become fully visible. The relief lasts only briefly. What remains is the conviction that she is always bracing for the next catastrophe and that other people do not understand how quickly a normal afternoon can turn.

Marisol finally sought help after a minor incident at work frightened her. A supervisor was late to a scheduled meeting, and during the unexpected quiet in the conference room she became so overwhelmed by the physical rush and the taste in her mouth that she had to leave abruptly and lock herself in a bathroom stall. She was embarrassed that she could not explain what had happened; even to herself, the experience still came more as sensations than words. What she fears most is that this miserable, cut-off version of her is permanent, that she will always be the person waiting for terrible news. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is to be able to remember what happened without feeling that danger is happening all over again.
